entry: Geological feature spanning parts of Central Asia, South Asia, West Asia, and the South Caucasus. The plateau, also called the Persian plateau, forms part of the Eurasian plate and is wedged between the Arabian and Indian plates. It stretches nearly 2,000 kilometres (1,200 mi) from the Caspian Sea to the Sulaiman Mountains and covers some 3,700,000 square kilometres (1,400,000 sq mi), most of it in [[Iran]] and [[Afghanistan]]. Its western boundary is the [[Zagros Mountains]]. Despite its name, the plateau is far from flat. If the eastern [[Hindu Kush]] is included, its highest point is Noshaq, at 7,492 metres (24,580 ft); its lowest is the Lut Desert, below 300 metres (980 ft) east of Kerman, Iran. The region's geology reflects the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian plates, and it is widely studied for that reason.

Country in West Asia (pop., 2024: 46.1 million), officially the Republic of Iraq. [[Baghdad]], home to over 8 million people, is the capital and largest city. The fertile plains between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, known as [[Mesopotamia]], were the site of early cities and empires, including Sumer and Assyria. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Iraq became the metropole of the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. It was governed within the [[Ottoman Empire]] from the 16th to the 20th century and gained independence in 1932 under a Hashemite monarchy. The Ba'ath Party took power in 1968, and under [[Saddam Hussein]] the country became a one-party state. Hussein fought a war against [[Iran]] from 1980 to 1988 and invaded [[Kuwait]] in 1990. The [[Iraq War]], which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003, toppled his government. Oil exports fund over 90 percent of federal revenues.

Protracted armed conflict in Iraq, lasting from 2003 to 2011 and also called the Second [[Gulf War]]. It began in March 2003 with an invasion by a United States-led coalition, which toppled the Ba'athist government of [[Saddam Hussein]]. Its main rationale, claims that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, proved false, and the 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence linking Saddam to [[Al-Qaeda]]. The fall of the regime created a power vacuum that fueled a sectarian civil war and an insurgency. A 2007 troop surge helped stabilize parts of the country, and U.S. combat troops withdrew in 2011. The war killed an estimated 150,000 to over a million people, including over 100,000 civilians. [[Kofi Annan]] called the invasion illegal under international law. The United States re-engaged in 2014 against the [[Islamic State]].

Island in the North Atlantic Ocean, in northwestern Europe. It is divided between the [[Republic of Ireland]], a sovereign state covering five-sixths of the island, and [[Northern Ireland]], part of the [[United Kingdom]]. The island is separated from [[Great Britain]] by the North Channel, the [[Irish Sea]], and St George's Channel, and it is the second-largest of the British Isles. Its population is just over 7 million as of 2022. Woodland covers about 10% of the island, compared with a European average of over 33%, and most of it is non-native conifer plantations. [[Vikings]] raided and settled the island from the late 8th to the early 11th centuries, until the Battle of Clontarf on 23 April 1014 led to the decline of Viking power. The Acts of Union in 1801 made Ireland part of the United Kingdom. Partition followed a war of independence, and the Irish Free State declared a republic in 1949. Both the Republic and the United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community in 1973.

Second-century Greek bishop and Church Father. Originating from Smyrna in [[Anatolia]], he had heard the preaching of Polycarp, who was said to have heard John the Evangelist. As a priest in [[Lyon]], he was sent to Rome in 177 with a letter to Pope Eleutherius, during a local persecution of Christians. He then succeeded the martyred Saint Pothinus as bishop of Lugdunum, now Lyon. His best-known work, *Against Heresies*, was written around 180 to refute [[Gnosticism]], particularly the teachings of Valentinus. He offered three pillars of orthodoxy: the scriptures, the tradition handed down from the apostles, and the teaching of the apostles' successors. He was the earliest surviving witness to regard all four of the now-canonical gospels as essential. Irenaeus is venerated as a saint in the [[Catholic Church]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], and [[Pope Francis]] declared him a Doctor of the Church in 2022.

Family of flowering plants in the order Asparagales, taking its name from the irises. It has a nearly global distribution, with 69 accepted genera and about 2500 species. Economically important cultivated members include species of Freesia, [[Gladiolus]], and Crocus, as well as the crop [[Saffron]]. The plants are perennials with a bulb, corm, or rhizome, and their leaves are generally grass-like with a sharp central fold. The family name comes from the genus Iris, which was coined in 1753 by Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]]. Subfamily Crocoideae is mainly African, and Isophysidoideae is monotypic, containing only Isophysis from Tasmania. Molecular clock analyses place the initial divergence in [[Antarctica]]-[[Australasia]] 82 million years ago.

Chemical element with atomic number 77 and symbol Ir. This very hard, brittle, silvery-white [[Transition metal]] of the [[Platinum]] group is the second-densest naturally occurring metal, after [[Osmium]]. It is one of the most corrosion-resistant metals, even at temperatures as high as 2,000 °C (3,600 °F). Smithson Tennant discovered it in 1803 in the acid-insoluble residues of platinum ores. Iridium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust, with an estimated annual production of only 6,800 kilograms (15,000 lb) in 2023. Its dominant uses are in high-performance spark plugs, crucibles for recrystallizing semiconductors at high temperatures, and electrodes for chlorine production. The unusually high iridium content of a clay layer at the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary]] gave rise to the Alvarez hypothesis of an impact that killed off non-avian dinosaurs, now linked to the [[Chicxulub crater]].

Genus of flowering plants with showy flowers, comprising 320 accepted species. It belongs to the family [[Iridaceae]], and iris is also a common name for all Iris species and some related genera. Some species are called flags, and the subgenus Scorpiris is widely known as junos in horticulture. Irises grow from creeping rhizomes or, in drier climates, from bulbs. The three usually drooping sepals are called falls, and some rhizomatous species have a fuzzy beard on each fall that guides pollinators to the nectar. The three upright petals are called standards. The name derives from the Greek word for rainbow. Three iris varieties feature in the flower data set that [[Ronald Fisher]] published in 1936 as an example of linear discriminant analysis.

Sea between [[Ireland]] and [[Great Britain]], covering 46,007 km² (17,763 sq mi). It separates Ireland, the [[Isle of Man]], and Great Britain, and it links to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] by the North Channel in the north and St George's Channel in the south. Anglesey, off North Wales, is its largest island. Its shores belong to Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland, and the Republic of Ireland. The sea is important for shipping, fishing, and power generation, including wind power and nuclear plants. Annual traffic between Great Britain and Ireland exceeds 12 million passengers and 17 million tonnes of traded goods. Because Ireland has no tunnel or bridge to Great Britain, most heavy goods trade crosses by sea. The sea was formed in the [[Neogene]] era, and Norman forces crossed it to invade Ireland in the late 12th century.

Guerrilla war fought in Ireland from 1919 to 1921 between the Irish Republican Army and British forces, including the Royal Irish Constabulary and the Auxiliaries. The conflict followed the [[Easter Rising]] and the landslide victory of Sinn Féin in the 1918 election. Bloody Sunday in [[Dublin]] in November 1920 led to an escalation of violence, and in December British forces burned the centre of [[Cork (city)|Cork]] in reprisal for an ambush. A ceasefire began on July 11, 1921. The Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 ended British rule in most of Ireland, but Northern Ireland remained part of the United Kingdom.

Celtic language indigenous to the island of Ireland, also called Irish Gaelic. It was the first language of most of the population until the 19th century, when English became dominant. Irish is the national and first official language of the [[Republic of Ireland]] and an official language of [[Northern Ireland]]. Ogham, dating from at least the 4th century AD, was replaced by the [[Latin script]] from the 5th century, and the language has one of the oldest vernacular literatures in Western Europe. Its three major dialects are Connacht, Munster, and Ulster Irish.

Political and physical boundary that divided [[Europe]] from the end of World War II in 1945 until the end of the [[Cold War]] in 1990/1991. East of the boundary, many small states were aligned with the [[Soviet Union]], which formally allied them in the [[Warsaw Pact]] in 1955, while most nations to the west were [[NATO]] members. The term first described physical barriers such as razor wire, fences, minefields, and watchtowers along the western border of the [[Eastern Bloc]]. Its origin is often attributed to a speech by [[Winston Churchill]] at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946. The most emblematic segment was the [[Berlin Wall]]. East Germany reunited with West Germany on October 3, 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

English heavy metal band. Formed in Leyton, East London, in 1975 by bassist and songwriter Steve Harris, the band is a pioneer of the new wave of British heavy metal. Its album *The Number of the Beast* (1982) is among the most popular heavy metal albums of all time, with almost 20 million copies sold. The band has sold over 130 million albums and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2026. For over 40 years its mascot, Eddie, has appeared on almost all its releases.

[[Marvel Comics]] superhero. Co-created by [[Stan Lee]] and designed by Don Heck and [[Jack Kirby]], the character is the alter ego of Anthony "Tony" Stark, an engineer who runs the weapons manufacturing company Stark Industries. The character was created in response to the [[Vietnam War]] as an attempt to make a likable pro-war figure. Early stories were set during the [[Cold War]], and later ones explored alcoholism and corporate espionage. Robert Downey Jr. played Stark in *Iron Man* (2008), the first film of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]].

Ore rich in iron, from which metallic iron can be economically extracted. Ores are usually rich in iron oxides such as [[Magnetite]] and [[Hematite]]. Iron ore is the raw material for [[Pig iron]], and about 98% of mined iron ore is used to make [[Steel]]. Iron is the fourth most abundant element in [[Earth's crust]], but it is mostly bound in silicate or carbonate minerals. Global production exceeds 2.5 billion metric tons a year, led by [[Australia]] and [[Brazil]].

Use of a heated iron to remove wrinkles and creases from [[Textile|fabric]]. Heating is commonly done to 180–220 °C (360–430 °F), depending on the fabric. Ironing loosens the bonds between long-chain [[Polymer|polymer]] molecules in the fibers. While the molecules are hot, the weight of the iron straightens the fibers, which keep their new shape as they cool. Some fabrics, such as [[Cotton|cotton]], need water added to loosen the bonds. The first known use of heated metal to iron clothes occurred in China. Permanent press clothing combines wrinkle-resistant [[Polyester]] with cotton to reduce the ironing needed. The electric iron was invented in 1882 by Henry W. Seely.

[[Real number]] that cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers. Among the best-known irrational numbers are [[Pi|π]], [[E (mathematical constant)|Euler's number e]], the [[Golden ratio|golden ratio]] φ, and the [[Square root|square root]] of two. Their decimal expansions neither terminate nor repeat, and any decimal that terminates or repeats must be rational. Geometrically, when the ratio of two line segments is irrational, the segments are incommensurable, sharing no common measure. The first proof of their existence is attributed to a Pythagorean, possibly Hippasus of Metapontum, who lived in the 5th century BC. They can also be written as non-terminating continued fractions, which in some cases are periodic. Almost all real numbers are irrational.

Principal river of [[Myanmar]]. Known in official romanization as the Ayeyarwady, it is about 2,170 km (1,350 mi) long, rising from the confluence of the N'mai and Mali rivers in Kachin State. It flows north to south and empties through the Irrawaddy Delta into the [[Andaman Sea]]. Its drainage basin of about 400,000 km² (156,000 mi²) covers 61% of the land area of Burma. The river has been used for trade since the sixth century, and an extensive network of [[Irrigation|irrigation]] canals supports agriculture. It remains Myanmar's largest commercial waterway. In 2007 the military government agreed to build seven hydroelectric dams, including the 3600 MW Myitsone Dam, which is no longer under construction. Environmental groups have raised concerns about the project's effect on the river's ecosystems, including the endangered Irrawaddy dolphin.

Class of [[Galaxy|galaxy]] without a distinct regular shape, unlike spiral or elliptical galaxies. Irregular galaxies are often chaotic in appearance, with neither a nuclear bulge nor any trace of spiral arm structure. They are thought to make up about a quarter of all galaxies, and a large share of the [[Local Group]] is irregular, mostly small dwarf irregulars. Irregular galaxies are commonly about one tenth the mass of the [[Milky Way]]. Some were once spiral or elliptical galaxies that were deformed by uneven external gravity, and some form in galaxy collisions. Their [[Star formation|star formation]] is both common and varied, shaped more by random gas motion than by density waves. The [[Large Magellanic Cloud]] was reclassified as a barred spiral, while the [[Small Magellanic Cloud]] remains an irregular galaxy.

Indian actor who worked in Hindi cinema as well as British and American films. He made his film debut in *Salaam Bombay!* (1988) and had his breakthrough as a leading actor with *Haasil* (2003) and *Maqbool* (2004). He won the National Film Award for Best Actor for the title role in *Paan Singh Tomar* (2011). Later films include *The Lunchbox* (2013) and *Piku* (2015), and Hollywood roles in *Life of Pi* (2012) and *Jurassic World* (2015). He received the Padma Shri in 2011.

Device used to irrigate agricultural crops, lawns, golf courses, and other areas. Sprinkler [[Irrigation|irrigation]] applies water in a controlled manner that mimics rainfall, through a network of pumps, valves, pipes, and sprinklers. Industrial rainguns operate at very high pressures and are also used for dust suppression and logging. Many industrial sprinklers are buried with their supporting [[Plumbing|plumbing]] and grouped into zones that a solenoid valve turns on and off. Home systems include impact, oscillating, and drip sprinklers, often on timers. Center-pivot irrigation was invented in 1940 by the farmer Frank Zybach of Strasburg, Colorado, and it transformed large-scale farming. Modern residential systems may use smart controllers and rain sensors to adjust watering to weather and soil moisture.

Functional gastrointestinal disorder marked by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits, which can recur over years. Its cause is unknown, and diagnosis rests on symptoms once other conditions have been ruled out. Treatment may include dietary changes, medication, and antidepressants such as [[Amitriptyline]], often at lower doses than those used for depression. The average global prevalence is 11.2%. In the [[Western world]] it is twice as common in women as men, but it does not affect life expectancy.

Russian-born American songwriter and composer whose music forms a large part of the Great American Songbook. Born in the [[Russian Empire]], he arrived in the United States at the age of five, after his family fled pogroms against the Jewish village of Tolochin. His first song, "Marie from Sunny Italy," was published in 1907, and his international hits began with "Alexander's Ragtime Band" in 1911. He could not read sheet music and was limited to playing the piano in the key of F♭, using a transposing lever for other keys. He wrote an estimated 1,500 songs, including scores for 20 original Broadway shows and 15 original Hollywood films. His songs include "God Bless America," "White Christmas," and "There's No Business Like Show Business." Berlin received an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]], a Grammy Award, a Tony Award, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1977.

American chemist, physicist, and metallurgical engineer. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1932 for his work in surface chemistry. His 1919 article on the arrangement of electrons in atoms built on [[Gilbert N. Lewis]]'s cubical atom theory, and he became embroiled in a priority dispute with Lewis over it. While at [[General Electric]] from 1909 to 1950, he invented the gas-filled [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent lamp]] and the [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] welding technique. He found that filling the bulb with an inert gas, such as [[Argon]], greatly lengthened the life of a [[Tungsten]] filament. He also improved the diffusion pump, which led to high-vacuum tubes. The Langmuir Laboratory for Atmospheric Research in New Mexico is named in his honor.

American film producer and head of production at [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] (MGM). Called "The Boy Wonder" for his youth and his talent for choosing scripts, actors, and production staff, he produced films including *Grand Hotel*, *China Seas*, *A Night at the Opera*, *Mutiny on the Bounty*, *Camille*, and *The Good Earth*. He was made head of MGM production in 1925, at age twenty-six, and during his twelve years there he produced some four hundred films. He introduced story conferences with writers, sneak previews, and extensive re-shooting of scenes. He coauthored the "Production Code," the morality guidelines followed by all studios, and he helped create stars including [[Greta Garbo]] and [[Clark Gable]]. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has periodically awarded its Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award since 1937 to producers whose films reflect consistently high quality.
